screens.title: Introduction to Deployment Pipelines & Networks
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying a smart contract is the moment your code becomes part of a shared, tamper-resistant ledger. In this lesson you will learn which Ethereum networks exist, why you choose one over another, and the concrete steps that turn compiled Solidity into bytecode and an Application Binary Interface that other tools can call. We will compare Mainnet, public testnets such as Sepolia, and local developer chains like the Hardhat Network, Ganache, and Anvil. You will also see a practical deployment script pattern used by mainstream tools and why gas costs and network congestion influence every deployment decision. By the end of this sequence you should be able to pick the right network for a stage of work, run a deployment to a local network for testing, and recognize common mistakes such as deploying to the wrong network or leaving private keys in source control. As you move through the lesson, notice the three core topics highlighted below — network choice, deployment steps, and cost management — each connects to a hands-on activity that will let you compile, deploy, and verify a small Greeter contract locally. Keep an eye out for safe key handling and storing ABI and address artifacts after deployment.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice so you can move from local tests to staged and production deployments safely. First, you will learn to differentiate Mainnet, public testnets like Sepolia, and local developer chains, and understand the tradeoffs of each. That skill helps you choose an environment that balances realism, cost, and speed. Second, you will understand the full deployment sequence: compilation to bytecode and ABI, signing transactions, funding an account, and waiting for mining confirmation. Knowing each step prevents surprises and failed deployments. Third, you will identify primary tools—Hardhat, Truffle, and Foundry—their roles in compiling, testing, and scripting deployments, and how a simple script automates repeated deployments. Each objective includes practice: run a local Hardhat node, deploy Greeter, examine the ABI and address, and then simulate a testnet deployment. These competencies prepare you to stage a contract on Sepolia before moving to Mainnet with confidence.

screens.title: Ethereum Network Types
screens.narratorSegment: An Ethereum network is an instance of the blockchain with its own ledger state and fee market. There are three practical categories you must distinguish. Mainnet is the canonical public Ethereum network where real value is exchanged; actions here are permanent and require real Ether. Public testnets, such as Sepolia, mimic Mainnet behavior while using valueless test ETH, which you can request from faucets. Testnets allow more realistic end-to-end testing, including interactions with other contracts and network latency, but they may experience congestion or intermittent instability. Local development chains like the Hardhat Network, Ganache, and Anvil run only on your machine. They give instant confirmations, reset capability, and deterministic behavior for fast iteration and debugging. A common misconception is that local networks fully replicate Mainnet behavior; they do not. Local chains are excellent for unit tests and quick iterations, while testnets are better for staging. When choosing, ask: do I need realistic timing and interaction with other services, or do I need speed and deterministic resets? For example, write and test complex logic and unit tests locally, then deploy the same compiled artifact to Sepolia to validate interoperability before any Mainnet deployment. This staged approach reduces risk and cost while providing meaningful verification.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Ethereum Network Types
Definition

Mainnet, Testnet, Local

A concise label: Mainnet is production; testnets like Sepolia are staging; local networks provide speed and control for development.

Mainnet — production, requires real ETH, transactions are immutable and costly.
Testnet (Sepolia) — realistic environment using test ETH, useful for staging and end-to-end testing.
Local network (Hardhat/Ganache/Anvil) — instant confirmations, full reset, great for quick iteration.
Why it matters
  • Choosing the wrong network risks spending real ETH or missing environment-specific bugs.
  • Testnets reveal issues like gas usage and interactions with external services without financial risk.
  • Local chains speed development but cannot guarantee Mainnet behavior under congestion.
Comparison
Mainnet
Real ETH, high costs, production safety required.
Sepolia
Test ETH, realistic latency, useful for staging.
Hardhat/Ganache
Instant blocks, resets, deterministic testing.
Key Takeaway

Use local networks for development speed, testnets for realistic staging, and Mainnet only after full verification and funding.

screens.title: Deployment Process Step-by-Step
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable deployment follows a clear sequence. First, compile your Solidity sources into bytecode and an ABI. The bytecode is the low-level instructions the Ethereum Virtual Machine executes; the ABI is a JSON description of the contract's public methods and events that front-ends and libraries use. Next, prepare constructor arguments and any initialization data. Then choose the target network and ensure your deployer account has sufficient funds for the expected gas cost. With artifacts and funds in place, create a transaction containing the contract bytecode and constructor parameters. This transaction must be signed with the deployer's private key. Signing can be performed locally using a development account or by a wallet provider for remote nodes. Once signed, send the transaction to the chosen network where it will be mined into a block. After a confirmation or several confirmations, the contract address becomes permanent and should be recorded alongside the ABI. A common misconception is that compilation or testing alone ensures a successful deployment; in practice, forgetting to fund the account, misconfiguring network endpoints, or passing wrong constructor arguments are common fail points. Always log the deployed address and save the ABI for frontend integration. In short: compile, prepare, fund, sign, send, confirm, and save artifacts.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Deployment Process
Steps
  1. Compile Solidity → generate bytecode and ABI.
  2. Prepare constructor arguments and initialize state if needed.
  3. Choose network and fund the deployer account with sufficient ETH or test ETH.
  4. Sign the deployment transaction with the deployer's private key.
  5. Send transaction, wait for mining and confirmations.
  6. Record contract address and save ABI for integration.
Common mistake
Deploying without funding the account or with incorrect constructor arguments often leads to failed transactions or contracts deployed in unusable states. Always verify parameters and balances before signing.
Visual flow
Source code —> Compiler —> Bytecode + ABI
Prepare args + Fund account
Sign transaction —> Send —> Mine & Confirm
Record address + Save ABI
Key Takeaway

Treat deployment as a transaction pipeline: missing any step can lead to failed or costly outcomes.

screens.title: A Basic Hardhat Deployment Script
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment scripts automate repeated tasks and reduce human errors. The canonical pattern used by Hardhat is to obtain the contract factory, call deploy with constructor arguments, wait for deployment to finish, and log the deployed address. This pattern handles compilation and links artifacts so your script is idempotent across runs. A common example deploy script obtains a signer from the configured provider, then uses getContractFactory to create a factory object and invoke deploy. The script waits for the returned deployed contract to signal it is mined and then prints the address. A useful extension is to output the artifact's ABI and address to a JSON file for front-end usage. A misconception is to expect deployment scripts to hide funding requirements; scripts still require the deployer account to have sufficient balance. Below you will see an example script used in many projects. Read it to understand the flow and notice where constructor arguments, signer selection, and post-deploy logs belong. After reading, consider how to add gas estimation or retries in high congestion conditions. A Basic Hardhat Deployment Script means use a deploy script that compiles, selects a signer, deploys with constructor args, waits for mining, logs address, and saves artifacts.. In practical terms, how a typical deploy.js compiles and deploys a token or simple contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use a deploy script that compiles, selects a signer, deploys with constructor args, waits for mining, logs address, and saves artifacts.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Hardhat deploy.js
Example Script
// scripts/deploy.js
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const [deployer] = await ethers.getSigners();

  console.log("Deploying contracts with the account:", deployer.address);
  console.log("Account balance:", (await deployer.getBalance()).toString());

  const MyToken = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyToken");
  const myToken = await MyToken.deploy("My Awesome Token", "MAT");

  await myToken.deployed();

  console.log("MyToken deployed to:", myToken.address);
}

main()
  .then(() => process.exit(0))
  .catch((error) => {
    console.error(error);
    process.exit(1);
  });
What to notice
  • getSigners returns accounts available to the configured provider; the first is used as deployer.
  • getContractFactory prepares compiled artifacts and a factory with deploy convenience.
  • deploy returns a contract instance; await deployed waits for mining confirmation.
Pro tip
Add logic to write the deployed address and ABI to a JSON file immediately after deployment. This makes front-end integration repeatable and avoids manual copy-paste errors.

screens.title: Greeter Contract and Local Deployment
screens.narratorSegment: A practical starting contract is Greeter. It stores a greeting and exposes a function to read and update it. This makes an excellent demo because it has constructor state, a view method, and a state-changing method. First, create the contract file and compile to produce artifacts. Then write a deploy script that deploys Greeter with an initial greeting. Run a local Hardhat node or just use the network provided by Hardhat in-process. When you execute the deploy script, you will see console output showing the deployer address, the account balance, and the deployed contract address. After deployment, call the greet function to confirm the initial value and then call setGreeting to change it and observe state mutation. A common misconception is that local deployments mirror Mainnet performance; they do not. However, they provide instant mining and easy debugging. When you run the local deploy, inspect the artifacts folder for the ABI and bytecode and save the deployed address. These artifacts are required for any front-end or integration test. This small workflow demonstrates the compile-to-deploy loop and gives predictable feedback for iterating on contract logic.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Greeter Lab Walkthrough
Contract
// contracts/Greeter.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

contract Greeter {
    string private _greeting;

    constructor(string memory greeting_) {
        _greeting = greeting_;
    }

    function greet() public view returns (string memory) {
        return _greeting;
    }

    function setGreeting(string memory greeting_) public {
        _greeting = greeting_;
    }
}
Deploy commands
Initialize the project, install Hardhat, add the contract, then run the deploy script with the local node. Example commands are provided in the lab activity and print the deployed address and initial greeting to the console for verification.
Check artifacts
After a successful deploy, inspect the artifacts directory to find the ABI JSON and the bytecode. Save the deployed address alongside the ABI for use by a front-end or integration tests.

screens.title: Mainnet vs Sepolia vs Hardhat Network
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing networks helps you select the right stage for work. Mainnet is the production environment; transactions move real value and require real Ether. Deploying here involves higher cost because storage and contract creation consume significant gas. Sepolia is a recommended public testnet that uses test ETH obtainable from faucets; it gives a closer approximation to Mainnet behavior including latency and gas fluctuation, although testnets may experience congestion or other anomalies. Hardhat Network is a local chain that runs on your machine and gives instant confirmations, predictable block times, and reset capability. Funding differs: Mainnet requires real Ether purchased through exchanges and transferred to your deployer account; Sepolia requires test ETH from faucets; Hardhat provides accounts funded by the local node with deterministic private keys. Transaction speed and cost tradeoffs are clear: Hardhat is fastest with no cost, Sepolia is slower and uses test ETH, and Mainnet is slowest and most expensive. A common misconception is that testnets are identical to Mainnet; they are not identical but they are the closest safe approximation for staging. Use Hardhat for rapid development, Sepolia for pre-production testing, and Mainnet only after verification and cost planning.

screens.title: Gas, Costs, and Network Congestion
screens.narratorSegment: Gas is the unit of computational work on Ethereum and every operation consumes some amount of it. Deploying a contract is often one of the most gas-intensive actions because the transaction stores bytecode on-chain. That storage and initialization cost means deployments will typically be much more expensive than simple transfers or function calls that only read state. Network congestion raises gas prices because the fee market moves with demand; when many users compete to include transactions, the base fee increases and miners or validators prioritize higher-fee transactions. To control costs, check current gas estimates before deploying and consider scheduling deployments during periods of lower activity. Another strategy is to estimate gas usage locally and set an appropriate gas limit so the transaction does not underprice. Remember that failed transactions can still consume gas and therefore cost money on public networks. A common misconception is that lowering the gas price always saves money; if the price is too low, the transaction may fail or be delayed indefinitely. Tools like gas trackers help you make informed choices, and testnets let you observe gas behavior without spending real ETH.

keyIdea.text: Deployments consume significant gas due to storing bytecode. Monitor gas prices and budget for higher costs during congestion.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Gas & Congestion
Concept

Why deployments cost more

Contract creation stores bytecode on-chain and may execute initialization logic, both of which consume more gas than simple transactions. Expect higher gas for complex contracts.

Estimate gas locally and compare with live gas trackers before deploying to public networks.
Consider deploying minimal proxy patterns or optimizing code if deployment size is a concern.
Remember: failed transactions still consume gas and cost money.
Mitigation strategies
  • Deploy during lower activity windows.
  • Use accurate gas estimation and provide an appropriate gas limit.
  • Test on Sepolia to observe likely gas patterns without spending real ETH.
Check your understanding
If you see a delayed transaction, is it always because of insufficient gas? Not necessarily. It can be due to a low gas price relative to the current base fee or temporary network congestion.

screens.title: Deployment Tools: Hardhat, Truffle, Foundry
screens.narratorSegment: Several frameworks streamline compiling, testing, and deploying smart contracts. Hardhat provides a flexible JavaScript-based environment, a built-in local network, task automation, and plugin support for tasks like gas reporting and contract verification. Truffle is an older framework with migration scripts and a CLI that automated deployments; it remains useful where its migration pattern fits a team's workflow. Foundry is a newer, fast toolkit written in Rust that focuses on fast compilation and native testing; it includes Anvil for local chain functionality. Each tool handles compilation and artifacts differently but serves the same core purpose: reduce manual steps and provide repeatable scripts you can run in CI. A common beginner mistake is assuming the same commands work identically across frameworks; configuration files differ and network setup must be adapted. For example, Hardhat uses hardhat. config. js to register networks and provider endpoints, whereas Foundry uses a different configuration approach. Pick a tool that matches your stack and team preferences, then learn its deployment script conventions to keep deployments repeatable and automatable. screens.title: Security, Artifacts, and Key Management
screens.narratorSegment: After a successful deployment, a few artifacts become essential: the contract address and the ABI. The address tells you where the contract lives; the ABI tells callers how to interact with it. Persist these artifacts in a project artifacts folder and check them into a secure release location so your front-end or integration tests can reference them. Equally important is private key management. Never hard-code your private keys in code or commit them to source control. Use environment variables, secret managers, or hardware wallets to sign transactions in production. A common beginner mistake is to store private keys in a repository or to forget to export the deployed address, forcing manual lookups later. For CI/CD, use ephemeral accounts or protected deployment pipelines with secrets stored securely. Also, add deployment logs that include the network name, deployer address, and transaction hash to make verification and troubleshooting simpler. These simple hygiene steps dramatically reduce risk and simplify subsequent integration and monitoring work. screens.title: Common Deployment Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Many deployment failures stem from a small set of avoidable mistakes. First, deploying to the wrong network happens when configuration points to a public network instead of a local chain; always double-check your network name and RPC endpoint before running a deployment. Second, insufficient funds cause transactions to fail or run out of gas; verify your deployer account balance and estimate the expected gas cost ahead of time. Third, exposing private keys in code or version control is a severe security error — use environment variables or secret managers and never commit. env files. Fourth, neglecting to save the deployed address and ABI creates friction for front-end integration; add automatic artifact exports in your deploy script. Finally, underestimating gas during congestion can lead to underpriced transactions that are dropped. When you encounter an error, examine the transaction hash and logs, check network status for congestion, and confirm the gas price and limit. A solid mitigation is to script pre-deployment checks: validate network name, confirm balance, and warn if gas estimates exceed a configurable threshold. These proactive checks prevent most common failures.

fullNarratorScript:
Deploying a smart contract is the moment your code becomes part of a shared, tamper-resistant ledger. In this lesson you will learn which Ethereum networks exist, why you choose one over another, and the concrete steps that turn compiled Solidity into bytecode and an Application Binary Interface that other tools can call. We will compare Mainnet, public testnets such as Sepolia, and local developer chains like the Hardhat Network, Ganache, and Anvil. You will also see a practical deployment script pattern used by mainstream tools and why gas costs and network congestion influence every deployment decision. By the end of this sequence you should be able to pick the right network for a stage of work, run a deployment to a local network for testing, and recognize common mistakes such as deploying to the wrong network or leaving private keys in source control. As you move through the lesson, notice the three core topics highlighted below — network choice, deployment steps, and cost management — each connects to a hands-on activity that will let you compile, deploy, and verify a small Greeter contract locally. Keep an eye out for safe key handling and storing ABI and address artifacts after deployment.

These objectives focus your practice so you can move from local tests to staged and production deployments safely. First, you will learn to differentiate Mainnet, public testnets like Sepolia, and local developer chains, and understand the tradeoffs of each. That skill helps you choose an environment that balances realism, cost, and speed. Second, you will understand the full deployment sequence: compilation to bytecode and ABI, signing transactions, funding an account, and waiting for mining confirmation. Knowing each step prevents surprises and failed deployments. Third, you will identify primary tools—Hardhat, Truffle, and Foundry—their roles in compiling, testing, and scripting deployments, and how a simple script automates repeated deployments. Fourth, you will recognize how gas and network congestion change deployment strategy and costs, and you will learn safe key management patterns so you never commit private keys to source control. Each objective includes practice: run a local Hardhat node, deploy Greeter, examine the ABI and address, and then simulate a testnet deployment. These competencies prepare you to stage a contract on Sepolia before moving to Mainnet with confidence.

This second objectives screen emphasizes practical competencies and safety. You will set up a minimal Hardhat project, create the Greeter contract, and write a deploy script that prints the deployed address and validates an initial state. Practically, that means running commands to initialize a project, installing development dependencies, and invoking the deploy script against a local chain. You will learn to read compiled artifacts including bytecode and ABI and understand why each is needed for frontends and contract interactions. Equally important is secure configuration: private keys must live in environment variables and never in committed files, and you should capture deployed addresses and ABI in a safe artifacts directory. Finally, confirm you can explain gas implications: why deployments cost more than simple transactions, how network congestion can increase fees, and at least one mitigation such as waiting or raising gas price estimation. These skills will be validated by deploying Greeter locally and by preparing a testnet deployment plan for Sepolia.

An Ethereum network is an instance of the blockchain with its own ledger state and fee market. There are three practical categories you must distinguish. Mainnet is the canonical public Ethereum network where real value is exchanged; actions here are permanent and require real Ether. Public testnets, such as Sepolia, mimic Mainnet behavior while using valueless test ETH, which you can request from faucets. Testnets allow more realistic end-to-end testing, including interactions with other contracts and network latency, but they may experience congestion or intermittent instability. Local development chains like the Hardhat Network, Ganache, and Anvil run only on your machine. They give instant confirmations, reset capability, and deterministic behavior for fast iteration and debugging. A common misconception is that local networks fully replicate Mainnet behavior; they do not. Local chains are excellent for unit tests and quick iterations, while testnets are better for staging. When choosing, ask: do I need realistic timing and interaction with other services, or do I need speed and deterministic resets? For example, write and test complex logic and unit tests locally, then deploy the same compiled artifact to Sepolia to validate interoperability before any Mainnet deployment. This staged approach reduces risk and cost while providing meaningful verification.

A reliable deployment follows a clear sequence. First, compile your Solidity sources into bytecode and an ABI. The bytecode is the low-level instructions the Ethereum Virtual Machine executes; the ABI is a JSON description of the contract's public methods and events that front-ends and libraries use. Next, prepare constructor arguments and any initialization data. Then choose the target network and ensure your deployer account has sufficient funds for the expected gas cost. With artifacts and funds in place, create a transaction containing the contract bytecode and constructor parameters. This transaction must be signed with the deployer's private key. Signing can be performed locally using a development account or by a wallet provider for remote nodes. Once signed, send the transaction to the chosen network where it will be mined into a block. After a confirmation or several confirmations, the contract address becomes permanent and should be recorded alongside the ABI. A common misconception is that compilation or testing alone ensures a successful deployment; in practice, forgetting to fund the account, misconfiguring network endpoints, or passing wrong constructor arguments are common fail points. Always log the deployed address and save the ABI for frontend integration. In short: compile, prepare, fund, sign, send, confirm, and save artifacts.

Deployment scripts automate repeated tasks and reduce human errors. The canonical pattern used by Hardhat is to obtain the contract factory, call deploy with constructor arguments, wait for deployment to finish, and log the deployed address. This pattern handles compilation and links artifacts so your script is idempotent across runs. A common example deploy script obtains a signer from the configured provider, then uses getContractFactory to create a factory object and invoke deploy. The script waits for the returned deployed contract to signal it is mined and then prints the address. A useful extension is to output the artifact's ABI and address to a JSON file for front-end usage. A misconception is to expect deployment scripts to hide funding requirements; scripts still require the deployer account to have sufficient balance. Below you will see an example script used in many projects. Read it to understand the flow and notice where constructor arguments, signer selection, and post-deploy logs belong. After reading, consider how to add gas estimation or retries in high congestion conditions. A Basic Hardhat Deployment Script means use a deploy script that compiles, selects a signer, deploys with constructor args, waits for mining, logs address, and saves artifacts.. In practical terms, how a typical deploy.js compiles and deploys a token or simple contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A practical starting contract is Greeter. It stores a greeting and exposes a function to read and update it. This makes an excellent demo because it has constructor state, a view method, and a state-changing method. First, create the contract file and compile to produce artifacts. Then write a deploy script that deploys Greeter with an initial greeting. Run a local Hardhat node or just use the network provided by Hardhat in-process. When you execute the deploy script, you will see console output showing the deployer address, the account balance, and the deployed contract address. After deployment, call the greet function to confirm the initial value and then call setGreeting to change it and observe state mutation. When you run the local deploy, inspect the artifacts folder for the ABI and bytecode and save the deployed address. These artifacts are required for any front-end or integration test. This small workflow demonstrates the compile-to-deploy loop and gives predictable feedback for iterating on contract logic.

Comparing networks helps you select the right stage for work. Mainnet is the production environment; transactions move real value and require real Ether. Deploying here involves higher cost because storage and contract creation consume significant gas. Sepolia is a recommended public testnet that uses test ETH obtainable from faucets; it gives a closer approximation to Mainnet behavior including latency and gas fluctuation, although testnets may experience congestion or other anomalies. Hardhat Network is a local chain that runs on your machine and gives instant confirmations, predictable block times, and reset capability. Funding differs: Mainnet requires real Ether purchased through exchanges and transferred to your deployer account; Sepolia requires test ETH from faucets; Hardhat provides accounts funded by the local node with deterministic private keys. A common misconception is that testnets are identical to Mainnet; they are not identical but they are the closest safe approximation for staging. Use Hardhat for rapid development, Sepolia for pre-production testing, and Mainnet only after verification and cost planning.

Deploying a contract is often one of the most gas-intensive actions because the transaction stores bytecode on-chain. That storage and initialization cost means deployments will typically be much more expensive than simple transfers or function calls that only read state. Remember that failed transactions can still consume gas and therefore cost money on public networks. A common misconception is that lowering the gas price always saves money; if the price is too low, the transaction may fail or be delayed indefinitely. Tools like gas trackers help you make informed choices, and testnets let you observe gas behavior without spending real ETH.

Keep three concise ideas in mind as you deploy: First, the network you choose — local, testnet, or Mainnet — determines cost, speed, and realism. Second, deployments are transactions that require compilation to bytecode and an ABI, signing with a funded account, and waiting for mining confirmations. Third, gas matters: deploying contracts uses significant gas, and network congestion can drive costs or cause underpriced transactions to fail. These core concepts guide safe deployment strategy: iterate locally, stage on Sepolia for realism, and deploy to Mainnet only after careful verification and budgeting.
